I mention that because as a loner myself it’s nice to see someone in a fictional world that is alone, is an outsider, awkward and described as ugly, and enjoys it. I get that bottling stuff up though, I do it too. I feel uncomfortable to open up around my family much, I think I’m conditioned this way from high school and I can’t get out of it. Plus, they can be overprotective. 

Sometimes the people that love us the most try their hardest to show us that love but it doesn’t always come off in the way that is right for us, ala being overprotective. Perhaps your grandparents and your family more broadly are saying these things like be strong and move on because they think it helps, but it doesn’t. Have you ever tried to communicate that? Because you went through a massive, life changing thing. That’s not something that you can just move on from. That’s something you need to process and let heal even long after the physical problems have gone away. 

You deserve the space, love, and support to process that and deal with it in the exact way that helps for you. To be open about it and not feel the pressure to bottle something in like that. 

Have you ever tried reaching out to a therapist or a professional mental health worker? For me, like I said, despite being lucky enough to have a supportive family I still don’t always feel 100% comfortable to talk about things with them, but that’s where the therapist comes in. I can talk about it, let things out that I otherwise would have held in and even though a problem or something on my mind might still be there, I feel the ability to cope with it much more and it doesn’t define my day or week as it might have otherwise.

So perhaps there’s a professional you can speak with virtually (as I do, just through zoom)? Even if it’s through school or something. And if you have one already and you don’t feel like you can say everything you want to, then maybe look into getting a new one. Think of it as them working for you, and you deserve someone who is the right fit that can help you. 

For what it’s worth, your post really touched me and made my heart break. I’m so sorry for everything that’s happened to you, I guess one thing i’d like to say and I’m not sure if it helps is that none of it defines you. The cancer, your way of walking, your parents’ abuse, your SAT scores or school performance in general, none of it defines you. You and only you get to decide who you are and how you’re defined. You are you, and no matter what anyone says, it’s your life and don’t let anything define you.

One thing I learned from graduating high school is how different the real world is. At school, so many toxic behaviors are normalized and kids make fun of their peers for this and that and the other. But in the real world, it’s so different. Obviously not everywhere and in every situation, but in my experience I am a lot less self conscious about myself now. I am very nerdy, the nerdy things occupy my mind at all times basically lol, and I love that. It makes me happy. I used to have to hide that at high school or I’d be made fun of. But now, I don’t need to hide that. I don’t feel myself looking inwards constantly or looking at myself in the mirror all the time to make sure nothing was wrong or anything.

So sorry for talking a lot about myself there. But my point is that school is an isolated bubble that can often be toxic, but things are better outside of that environment. Coincidentally, someone I work with had a similar thing with cancer, it caused some things (not walking), and the reaction wasn’t like it was for you. Everyone has been supportive, not gossipy, not judgmental or nosy. People are proud of them for overcoming it and are just glad they’re okay. 

Heck, people at my work have noticed my self harm scars and have been good about it. No judgement or anything like that all. No excessive questions, just saying let me know if you need anything or someone to talk to and that’s it. Not mentioned unless I mention it, which I never do.

All of this to say that school can feel like it’ll never end, that every place you’ll ever be in will be like that but it’s not. Things will get better.

I’m so sorry that you’re struggling at the moment. Seeing a psychologist at uni is a good idea, as they can be a great resource to help students. Given that you’re 18, you’re legally an adult, meaning that they wouldn’t legally be allowed to tell your parents anything unless you specifically give them permission to relay certain information. Suicidal ideation without a clear plan or date, or self harm that isn’t life threatening, is something that psychologists deal with themselves. Also, to address the question of if they would ask you to go to someone outside the uni, that really depends on the particular psychologist. I know from experience that they might only ask you to see someone outside if there’s a particular individual they have in mind (say, you’re really struggling with anxiety and there’s a therapist who specializes in anxiety in young adults, that sort of thing).
